name: HU6
lead: HU6 is an investigational once-daily oral drug from Rivus Pharmaceuticals. It is a prodrug of 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a mitochondrial uncoupler, and was designed to give steadier blood concentrations than DNP itself.[1][2] Rivus calls this class of drug a controlled metabolic accelerator.[3]

For appearance, the relevance is body composition: the mechanism raises energy expenditure so that fat is oxidised rather than stored, and the published trials track liver fat, body weight, fat mass and visceral fat. In a 19-week heart-failure trial, HU6 produced a larger fall in fat mass than placebo with no significant loss of muscle mass.[12] Online, DNP has a long history as a bodybuilding and cutting compound, and HU6 is sometimes discussed as a regulated successor to it.[2]

DNP was sold for weight loss in the 1930s and then withdrawn because of toxicity; it is associated with fatal overdoses.[2] HU6 is a separate, investigational molecule that has been tested in phase 1 and phase 2 trials in obesity-related liver disease, overweight and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF).[3][12] It is not approved anywhere and is not sold as a product.
infobox: DNP prodrug; mitochondrial uncoupler (controlled metabolic accelerator)

paras: HU6 belongs to the mitochondrial-uncoupler family. Its developer describes it as a controlled metabolic accelerator, a drug that increases metabolic rate and substrate use so that fat and other carbon sources are burned instead of accumulating in the liver and other tissues.[3] Taking HU6 under fasting conditions was part of the liver-fat trial design.[3]

Rivus describes itself as a clinical-stage cardiometabolic company. Its announcements name HU6 as its lead candidate for MASH (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, formerly NASH) and list a separate preclinical oral GLP-1 agonist, RV-8451, in development for obesity.[13]

Excess fat, especially visceral and liver fat, is the target of every HU6 trial. Reductions in fat mass without loss of muscle, as seen in the HFpEF study, are the outcome that physique-focused readers associate with a cutting agent.[12] No trial has enrolled lean or normal-weight people, and no study has measured appearance outcomes.
Registered trials examine fatty liver disease (NAFLD, NASH and MASH), obesity-related HFpEF, and overweight volunteers.[3][4][8][9][10]

The phase 2a trial (NCT04874233) was randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled at a single US site. It enrolled 80 adults aged 28-65 with BMI 28-45 and at least 8% liver fat by MRI-PDFF, who took HU6 or placebo once daily for 61 days. The primary endpoint was relative change in liver fat.[3][4]

Mean liver fat fell by 26.8% (150 mg), 35.6% (300 mg) and 33.0% (450 mg), versus a 5.4% increase on placebo. No serious treatment-emergent adverse events or deaths were reported. Flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations were the most common events in HU6 groups. Three HU6 participants and two placebo participants stopped for adverse events.[3] The trial was funded by Rivus.[3]

The HuMAIN-HFpEF study (NCT05284617) was a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled dose-escalation trial in adults with chronic stable HFpEF and obesity. Of 66 participants randomised (mean age 64.5, 58% female), 56 completed 19 weeks, starting at 150 mg per day with possible up-titration to 450 mg per day. The primary endpoint was body weight.[12][8]

HU6 lowered body weight by about 2.9 kg more than placebo (95% CI -4.68 to -1.04), total fat mass by about 3.0 kg more, and visceral fat percentage by about 1.3 points, with no significant loss of muscle mass. Peak VO2, six-minute walk distance, quality-of-life score and NT-proBNP did not change significantly. Five participants had serious adverse events (four on HU6, one on placebo, including one death), all judged unrelated to treatment. The authors concluded that the weight loss was modest and that larger, longer trials are needed to see whether exercise capacity and outcomes improve.[12]

Other registered studies include phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic trials (NCT04463017, NCT04709913, NCT05433506, NCT06325930, NCT07170189), a phase 2 study in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (NCT05284617), a phase 2 study in NASH (NCT05979779) and a phase 2 MASH study that was recruiting in 2026 (NCT07491458). A phase 2a energy-metabolism study in type 2 diabetes (NCT06104358) was withdrawn.[4][5][6][7][8][9][10][11]

A larger phase 2 trial in NASH (NCT05979779, n=219) is listed as active and not recruiting, and a 180-person MASH trial began in February 2026.[9][10] Phase 1 studies include a 2025 trial in overweight people (n=59) and a 2024 absorption, metabolism and excretion study with radiolabelled drug.[14][15]
HU6 is metabolised in the liver to DNP, which shuttles protons across the mitochondrial membrane and dissipates the gradient that drives ATP production, releasing energy as heat.[2]

The liver-fat trial states that HU6 is metabolised in the liver to DNP, so DNP is the active uncoupler.[3] Uncoupling raises energy expenditure because energy that would have made ATP is lost as heat. Controlled-release delivery is intended to keep concentrations in a narrower range than DNP tablets, which can cause rapid heating and overdose.[2]

DNP is banned for human consumption by the FDA, is banned by WADA since 2015, and was reclassified in the UK as a regulated poison in October 2023. Wikipedia reports that bodybuilders and people with eating disorders obtain it online, and that at least 50 overdose deaths were reported worldwide between 2010 and 2020.[2] HU6 is a distinct, investigational prodrug and is not the same product.

In online physique communities DNP is discussed as a powerful cutting compound, and its use is associated with fatal overdoses reported by health authorities and Wikipedia.[2] HU6 is mentioned in those discussions as a pharmaceutical-grade relative, but it is available only to trial participants.

In the phase 2a liver trial, flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations were the most common events in HU6 groups; no serious treatment-emergent adverse events or deaths were reported, and five participants withdrew for adverse events (three HU6, two placebo).[3] The HFpEF trial reported serious events in both arms, judged unrelated to treatment.[12] Safety in larger, longer trials is still being collected.[9][10]

timeline.event: DNP sold for weight loss, later withdrawn for toxicity.[2]
Phase 2a results published in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology; NASH phase 2 begins.[3][9]
HuMAIN-HFpEF results published in JAMA Cardiology.[12]

card.summary: An experimental, slow-release prodrug of the toxic fat-burner DNP, still in phase 2 trials.
card.note: Unapproved; DNP itself is associated with fatal overdoses.

quick.overview:
HU6 is an experimental pill from Rivus Pharmaceuticals designed to deliver DNP, a historic weight-loss uncoupler, in a more controlled way. It is in phase 2 trials for fatty liver, obesity and heart failure.

A 2023 phase 2a trial of 80 people reported reduced liver fat versus placebo over 61 days.
quick.mechanism: After being converted to DNP in the liver, it lets mitochondria lose energy as heat instead of making ATP.
quick.risks: Flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations were most common in the trial. It is unapproved, and DNP itself has caused fatal overdoses and is banned for human consumption.
